definition: The task of identifying inputs that differ significantly from the distribution of data a model was trained on, so the system can flag uncertainty or defer to a human.
details: OOD detection is important for safe deployment, helping systems recognize when they are being asked to operate outside their reliable competence and should respond with caution or abstain.

explainer.lead: Out-of-distribution detection identifies inputs that differ substantially from what a model was trained on, so the system can flag uncertainty or hand off to a human. It is a safeguard for deploying models in open-ended settings.

tiers.eli5: It's like a doctor noticing a symptom that doesn't match anything they learned and saying 'I should get a specialist' instead of guessing.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers attach OOD scores or thresholds so the system abstains or escalates when inputs look unfamiliar. The pitfall is calibration: a threshold that catches real anomalies often also flags legitimate rare inputs.
tiers.paperLevel: Given training distribution P and input x, decide whether x was drawn from P; typical approaches score distributional distance and threshold it. No single score is reliable across all shifts.

explainer.example: A classifier trained on cats and dogs receives a photo of a car; the OOD detector flags it and the system asks for human review rather than forcing a cat/dog label.
